paragraphs: This paper addresses how to choose the basis elements used in a sparse Gaussian process regression model. A sparse model represents predictions through a selected collection of elements, making the selection criterion important for both computational effort and predictive quality. The authors propose a new criterion, framed in the title as a matching pursuit approach.

The contribution concerns the tradeoff between building a compact model efficiently and retaining useful predictions. The abstract reports promising gains in both accuracy and efficiency over earlier methods. Its comparisons are specific: the proposed algorithm is much faster than the method of Smola and Bartlett, while its generalization substantially exceeds that of the information gain approach of Seeger and colleagues.

The reported generalization advantage is especially strong for the quality of predictive distributions. This matters because a regression model can describe a range of plausible outcomes as well as a single predicted value. The stated findings therefore concern both computational practicality and the quality of the probabilistic predictions produced by the selected sparse representation.
neurips-2005-a-matching-pursuit-approach.tldr: A new basis selection criterion for sparse Gaussian process regression reports faster computation and improved generalization relative to specific earlier methods.

paragraphs: Spectral clustering uses relationships among data points to organize them into groups. The paper identifies two difficulties with many existing algorithms: handling multiple clusters requires additional strategies, and hard membership decisions can leave optimization trapped at a local optimum. These issues motivate a more flexible treatment of which groups a point belongs to.

The proposed algorithm, Soft Cut, modifies normalized cut by introducing soft cluster membership. Instead of expressing membership solely through an exclusive assignment, it allows a probabilistic treatment. This changes the clustering formulation so that membership can remain flexible during optimization, directly addressing the concern about hard assignments raised by the authors.

The authors use a bound optimization algorithm to compute Soft Cut efficiently and report promising results across a variety of datasets. The contribution combines a different treatment of membership with a practical optimization procedure. The experimental findings support the usefulness of that combination, while the abstract does not claim that soft membership guarantees avoidance of every local optimum.
neurips-2005-a-probabilistic-approach-fo.tldr: Soft Cut introduces probabilistic membership into normalized-cut clustering and uses efficient bound optimization, with promising experimental results.

paragraphs: The paper studies how a population of noisy coding units can preserve a high-quality sensory signal. It frames this as transmitting a multidimensional analog signal through noisy channels. Earlier work learned robust representations by reducing reconstruction error while constraining channel capacity; this paper develops a theoretical account of the resulting coding problem.

The analysis characterizes optimal linear encoders and decoders for one-dimensional and two-dimensional data. It permits any number of coding units, covering representations with fewer or more units than input dimensions. Within this setting, it shows how the optimal code changes with the number of units, the data, and the noise conditions to achieve robustness.

The authors also report numerical solutions for higher-dimensional image data. Those image codes are substantially more robust in the reported comparisons with ICA and wavelet codes. The theoretical and numerical contributions have distinct scopes: the explicit optimality analysis concerns low-dimensional linear coding, while the image results demonstrate the robustness of numerical solutions in a larger setting.
neurips-2005-a-theoretical-analysis-of-r.tldr: The paper characterizes optimal low-dimensional linear codes under noise and reports robust numerical codes for higher-dimensional images.

paragraphs: Active learning chooses where to obtain training examples with the aim of reducing prediction error on new data. This paper examines what happens when the chosen regression model cannot exactly express the function being learned. Such model misspecification matters because a strategy for choosing informative inputs may rely on assumptions that the model itself violates.

The authors first show that an existing active learning method has a theoretical justification under a weaker condition than exact model correctness. Some slight misspecification is allowed. They then argue that this relaxed condition remains restrictive in practice and propose an alternative method with a justification covering a wider class of misspecified models.

The supplied formulation evaluates regression through expected squared test error, with fixed basis functions and independent, zero-mean observation noise. Numerical studies show that the proposed selection method is robust to model misspecification. Together, the theory and experiments support a broader range of applications, without asserting that the method handles every possible mismatch between a model and its target.
neurips-2005-active-learning-for-misspec.tldr: A new active learning method has theoretical support for a wider class of misspecified regression models and shows robustness in numerical studies.

paragraphs: Bayesian Sets addresses retrieval by example: a user supplies a few items belonging to a concept or cluster, and the system seeks additional members. The central challenge is turning those examples into a ranking of candidates. The paper treats this as Bayesian inference using a model-based definition of what constitutes a cluster.

Each candidate receives a score evaluating the marginal probability that it belongs to a cluster containing the query items. For exponential family models with conjugate priors, this calculation reduces to a simple function of sufficient statistics. For the sparse binary data emphasized in the paper, the score can be computed exactly with one sparse matrix multiplication, enabling application to very large datasets.

The evaluation covers movie retrieval from EachMovie, completion of author sets from NIPS data, and completion of word sets from the Grolier encyclopedia. The authors also compare against Google Sets and report very reasonable completions. These results illustrate the use of the same probabilistic retrieval formulation across several kinds of items.
neurips-2005-bayesian-sets-9b01dfb056.tldr: Bayesian Sets ranks candidates for example-based set completion using a probabilistic cluster score that is especially efficient for sparse binary data.

paragraphs: Support vector regression includes a regularization choice that influences the fitted model. Rather than producing only the fit associated with one choice, this paper derives an algorithm for computing the entire solution path. The path describes how the regression solution changes as the regularization parameter varies, making a family of possible fits available together.

The main computational claim is that obtaining this full path costs essentially as much as fitting a single support vector regression model. This makes the path useful for exploring the regularization choice without treating every candidate setting as an unrelated fitting problem. The word essentially qualifies the cost comparison; the abstract presents an overall computational advantage rather than an exact equality of running times.

The paper also proposes an unbiased estimate of the model's degrees of freedom, a way to describe its effective flexibility. This estimate supports convenient selection of the regularization parameter. The two contributions work together: the solution path supplies the candidate fits, while the degrees-of-freedom estimate helps guide the choice among them.
neurips-2005-computing-the-solution-path.tldr: The paper computes the full support vector regression solution path at roughly single-fit cost and supplies an unbiased degrees-of-freedom estimate for regularization selection.

paragraphs: This paper asks how much earlier text a language model should use as context. A long history can contain useful information, but the subject of a passage can change. Treating that history as an unordered bag of words does not explicitly account for when those changes occurred or which portion of the history is currently relevant.

The authors model topic shifts as an unobserved stochastic process within a probabilistic generative model. The model has partial exchangeability, combining some freedom to reorder observations with structure that preserves relevant distinctions. An online particle-filtering algorithm infers topic changes as text arrives and uses that inference to select an appropriate context length automatically.

Experiments on the BNC corpus show consistent improvement over previous methods that ignore chronological order. The finding supports the value of tracking topic changes when deciding which earlier text should inform a prediction. More broadly, the paper presents context selection as an inference problem about a changing hidden process, connecting long-distance language modeling with the modeling of discrete sequences.
neurips-2005-context-as-filtering-aab99e.tldr: A probabilistic model of topic shifts uses online particle filtering to adapt context length and improves results over order-insensitive methods on the BNC corpus.

paragraphs: The paper revisits the relationship between neural network training and convex optimization. The authors begin from the concern that nonconvexity is a disadvantage of many learning methods, including multilayer neural networks. Their central result is that training can be viewed as a convex optimization problem when the number of hidden units is itself learned.

That reformulation introduces an infinite number of variables. The paper therefore pairs its conceptual result with a way to construct a solution incrementally. The procedure inserts one hidden unit at a time, with each insertion requiring a linear classifier that minimizes a weighted sum of errors. The growing network provides a route for working with the otherwise infinite formulation.

The significance lies in linking representation size and optimization: learning how many hidden units to use is part of the convex view. The result concerns this formulation and its unit-insertion procedure, rather than a blanket statement about every neural network training setup. It shows how a seemingly difficult optimization problem can take a different form when the representation is allowed to grow.
neurips-2005-convex-neural-networks-d7f1.tldr: Learning the number of hidden units permits a convex formulation of neural network training that can be solved by adding units incrementally.

paragraphs: Neural firing patterns can change rapidly as network excitability or an animal's behavioral state changes. This paper develops a method for recovering the timing of such hidden state changes from recordings of one or more neurons. It uses the intervals between spikes to connect the observed activity with the underlying state dynamics.

The algorithm maximizes the likelihood of the recorded spike trains by jointly optimizing state lifetimes and the distribution of interspike intervals within each state. Its nonparametric formulation avoids the time-binning and spike-counting problems identified by the authors. Its computational complexity matches that of a mixed-state Markov model operating on a sequence whose length equals the total number of recorded spikes.

As an example, the authors fit a two-state model to paired recordings of premotor neurons in a sleeping songbird. The interval distributions associated with the two inferred states closely resemble those measured during waking and singing, respectively. This finding links distinct patterns recovered during sleep to patterns observed in those other conditions, through their spike-interval statistics.
neurips-2005-efficient-estimation-of-hid.tldr: A likelihood-based algorithm infers hidden neural state dynamics directly from spike intervals, with a songbird example revealing distributions resembling waking and singing activity.

paragraphs: Many uses of graphical models depend on estimating how strongly variables inform one another. Such calculations help with tasks including active learning and sensitivity analysis. The paper focuses on their computational cost: previous pairwise information-gain calculations required work growing quadratically with network size, which makes them increasingly expensive as a model grows.

The authors show how to perform a similar information-value computation with cost growing linearly in network size. The key is a loss function whose form permits dynamic programming. That structure leads to a message-passing algorithm, allowing the calculation to exploit the organization of the graphical model. The claim concerns this suitable formulation rather than every possible information-gain calculation.

Empirical results show large speedups without reduced accuracy. In the cost-sensitive domains examined, the method also achieves better accuracy. These findings give the computational change practical significance: the proposed information-value calculation was substantially cheaper while preserving, and in those cost-sensitive settings improving, the reported quality of the resulting decisions.
neurips-2005-fast-information-value-for-.tldr: A dynamic-programming-compatible loss enables linear-cost information-value calculations, with large empirical speedups and no reported accuracy decrease.

paragraphs: Batch learning and online learning place different demands on a learner. In the batch setting described here, examples are drawn independently from a distribution. In the online setting, an arbitrary sequence must be labeled one example at a time. The paper starts from the known direction that online learnability implies batch learnability and investigates a converse.

The authors provide an efficient procedure for converting a batch learning algorithm into an online one. The conversion is transductive: it has access to future examples without their labels. That access is a central condition of the result, because it gives the learner information about inputs it will later need to label while keeping their answers unknown.

The result establishes an equivalence between proper, efficient learnability in the batch model and in this transductive online model. Here, proper learning concerns predictions represented within the designated hypothesis class. The contribution clarifies how future unlabeled data can connect the two learning settings; it does not remove the transductive condition to establish the same equivalence for unrestricted online learning.
neurips-2005-from-batch-to-transductive-.tldr: An efficient conversion establishes equivalence between proper, efficient batch learning and online learning with access to future unlabeled inputs.

paragraphs: The study asks whether activity in human extrastriate visual cortex distinguishes individual object images, extending beyond the previously demonstrated decoding of object categories. The authors collect fMRI responses to 12 distinct images and examine information distributed across voxels, the spatial measurement units in the scans.

A simple winner-take-all classifier uses half of each recording session's data for training. Because noisy voxels can interfere with this approach, the authors compare two ways to select informative subsets. One measures how reliably a voxel responds across subsets of the data. The other estimates its mutual information with the stimulus set, assessing how informative its response is about the presented image.

Both selection criteria identify subsets that reliably encode object identity, including when artificial noisy measurements are added. Mutual information is less efficient for this task, which the authors suggest is likely related to constraints of fMRI data. The results support the presence of decodable information about these individual images and show why choosing useful measurements matters for recovering it.
neurips-2005-identifying-distributed-obj.tldr: Two voxel-selection methods recover reliable information about 12 individual object images from extrastriate fMRI activity, even with added noisy measurements.

paragraphs: This paper studies inference when communication inside a directed graphical model is severely restricted. Hidden nodes are binary, observations are noisy real values, and each node may broadcast exactly one bit only to its children. The task is to choose either the most probable joint hidden assignment or the most probable value of each hidden node.

The authors treat the local processing rules at all nodes as quantities to optimize. Their variational formulation seeks to minimize the loss in expected inference performance caused by the communication restriction. This makes the design decision explicit: each node must compress what it knows into one bit, and the usefulness of that bit depends on the rules used elsewhere.

The resulting message-passing algorithm runs offline, before observations arrive. It iteratively coordinates the local rules using global statistical information, reducing the performance loss when the constrained online communication later occurs. The paper supplies illustrative examples and assumptions guaranteeing convergence and efficiency. Those guarantees are conditional on the stated assumptions, while the one-bit restriction defines the inference problem throughout.
neurips-2005-inference-with-minimal-comm.tldr: Offline variational optimization coordinates local inference rules to reduce expected performance loss when each graphical-model node can send only one bit to its children.

paragraphs: The paper learns to estimate scene depth from a single image. Its training data pair monocular photographs with corresponding ground-truth depth maps, covering unstructured outdoor environments such as forests, trees, and buildings. Supervised learning then connects the appearance of an image to the depth values the model should predict.

The authors emphasize that local image features alone do not provide enough information to estimate depth at a point. Their discriminatively trained Markov random field therefore incorporates image features at multiple scales, including both local evidence and global context. It models individual depth values together with relationships between depths at different image locations.

This combination matters because depth predictions at separate points need to be interpreted in the context of the wider scene. The reported results show that the algorithm frequently recovers fairly accurate depth maps, even for unstructured scenes. The finding supports the usefulness of learning contextual and relational information for monocular depth estimation, with the stated success remaining frequent and approximate rather than universal or exact.
neurips-2005-learning-depth-from-single-.tldr: A supervised Markov random field combines multiscale image context and depth relationships to frequently recover fairly accurate depth maps from single outdoor images.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a probabilistic approach to learning several related tasks together. Its central assumption is that the parameters for those tasks arise from hidden independent sources. Shared sources provide an explanation for why tasks are related, making the structure behind their parameters part of the model rather than treating every task in isolation.

The approach builds on independent component analysis and assigns Laplace distributions to the hidden sources. The authors state that this allows identification of the independent components, going beyond a description of correlations among tasks. The model also has a sparsity property, which they associate with a compact representation and robustness.

The authors develop efficient algorithms for empirical Bayes learning and for point estimation. Experiments on two multi-label text classification datasets give promising results. The contribution therefore includes both a model of task relationships and ways to fit it. Its interpretation depends on the independent-source assumption: the hidden components are the proposed mechanism through which information about related tasks is organized and shared.
neurips-2005-learning-multiple-related-t.tldr: A sparse probabilistic model explains related tasks through independent Laplace-distributed sources and shows promising results on two text classification datasets.

paragraphs: This paper learns helicopter dynamics from recorded sequences of states and actions. It addresses two questions: how to represent the vehicle's motion and how to train a model for predictions extending beyond the next time step. Both matter when the goal is to predict how a vehicle will evolve over an extended sequence.

The authors show that the linear parameterization used in models such as those learned by CIFER makes properties including inertia fundamentally difficult to capture. They propose an acceleration-based parameterization that avoids this deficiency while remaining equally efficient to learn from data. The contribution changes the representation of the dynamics without requiring a less efficient learning procedure.

The second contribution is an efficient algorithm that approximately minimizes prediction error over long time scales. This targets a different objective from explicitly modeling only one-step transitions in a Markov decision process. The paper presents empirical results on two helicopters and argues that the ideas also apply to broad classes of vehicle dynamics, although the reported applications concern those helicopters.
neurips-2005-learning-vehicular-dynamics.tldr: An acceleration-based dynamics model addresses inertia-related shortcomings of linear parameterizations, while a second algorithm targets longer-term prediction error.

paragraphs: The paper develops a measure of coordination in neuronal spike trains. Neural populations can represent stimuli through changing sequences of activity, so the authors seek a statistic that captures information sharing in those dynamics. Their proposed informational coherence asks how much better one unit can be predicted when the dynamical state of another is known.

To obtain those dynamical states, the method uses an algorithm that reconstructs effective state spaces from stochastic time series. This makes the inferred state of each unit central to the comparison. The authors argue that informational coherence provides a better measure of association and shared information than traditional pairwise synchronization and correlation measures.

The approach also extends beyond pairs by estimating network multi-information, allowing a multivariate analysis of shared activity. The authors illustrate the method on a detailed model of a transition from gamma to beta rhythms. This application demonstrates how the proposed analysis can be used to study changing network coordination, with the abstract presenting the broader superiority claim as an argument by the authors.
neurips-2005-measuring-shared-informatio.tldr: Informational coherence measures neural coordination through improved prediction from another unit's dynamical state and extends to network-wide information sharing.

paragraphs: This paper uses dynamic Bayesian networks to model interactions among active brain regions measured with fMRI. The networks serve as generative models of brain activation patterns, with an application to neuronal circuits associated with reward. The objective is to study how regions interact through time, extending the analysis beyond which regions are active.

The authors compare four model types: parallel, coupled, fully linked, and dynamically multi-linked hidden Markov models. They also propose and compare two learning schemes for the dynamically multi-linked version. Models inferred from fMRI data are evaluated through a group classification task, testing whether their interaction patterns carry information that distinguishes the studied groups.

The experiments show that classification can be performed using networks constructed from as few as five brain regions. The proposed learning methods also produce different network structures for drug-addicted and control subjects. The authors present these differences as an independent test of psychopathology's relationship with brain function, grounding their interpretation in modeled interactions and the reported group-level classification results.
neurips-2005-modeling-neuronal-interacti.tldr: Dynamic Bayesian networks model reward-related fMRI interactions and reveal structures that distinguish drug-addicted subjects from controls in a group classification task.

paragraphs: This paper addresses density estimation when high dimensionality makes nearby training examples scarce. The authors argue for learning non-local functions: the value and shape of a function at one location should be inferred using examples that may be far away. Their proposed nonparametric density estimator is designed around this use of information beyond the immediate neighborhood.

The estimator builds on Gaussian mixture models whose covariance matrices are regularized to reflect the local shape of a manifold. That shape describes how the data are arranged near a location. The method also draws on non-local estimators of manifold tangent planes, which characterize the local directions in which the manifold extends.

The important connection is that local geometric structure can itself be inferred non-locally. The cited tangent-plane estimators can generalize in regions containing little training data, unlike the traditional local nonparametric models discussed by the authors. The paper combines these ideas into a density estimator motivated by escaping the curse of dimensionality; the abstract presents that motivation as a claim, rather than a universal guarantee.
neurips-2005-non-local-manifold-parzen-w.tldr: A non-local density estimator combines manifold-shaped Gaussian components with geometry inferred from potentially distant examples to address sparse high-dimensional data.

paragraphs: Brain-computer interfaces can distinguish imagined movements using changes in EEG activity over sensorimotor cortex. The paper notes that widely used amplitude-based approaches, including Common Spatial Patterns, do not incorporate the richer phase dynamics of EEG rhythms. It investigates whether a measure of synchronization events can provide useful information for recognizing motor imagery.

The proposed feature is phase synchrony rate. It is calculated from a binarized phase-locking value and counts discrete synchronization events within a time window. Nonparametric statistical tests find significant differences in these rates between two kinds of motor imagery. Classifiers trained on the rates consistently produce results described as satisfactory across all five subjects.

For three subjects, phase information is more discriminative than amplitude during the first 1.5 to 2 seconds. This timing result suggests that phase could help improve information transfer rates in brain-computer interfaces. The conclusion is a possibility supported by early discrimination in those subjects, rather than a demonstrated increase in transfer rate for every participant.
neurips-2005-phase-synchrony-rate-for-th.tldr: Phase synchrony rates distinguish two motor-imagery types, with early phase advantages in three of five subjects suggesting potential for faster BCI communication.

paragraphs: Fisher linear discriminant analysis can be sensitive to the data used to define a classification problem. This paper addresses that sensitivity by explicitly modeling uncertainty in the problem data. The robust version optimizes for the worst case permitted by the uncertainty model, making the assumed range of variation part of the classification procedure.

The main result is that robust Fisher analysis can be performed through convex optimization for general convex uncertainty models. This supplies a tractable formulation for a broad class of uncertainty descriptions. For a particular product-form model of uncertainty, the authors further show that the computational cost can be comparable to ordinary Fisher analysis.

Numerical examples demonstrate the method, and the authors extend the results to kernel Fisher discriminant analysis in a high-dimensional feature space. The contribution links robustness with an explicit optimization framework. Its protection is defined relative to the chosen uncertainty model, and the especially favorable cost comparison applies to the specified product-form case rather than every convex uncertainty model.
neurips-2005-robust-fisher-discriminant-.tldr: Robust Fisher analysis handles convex data uncertainty through convex optimization, with standard-LDA-like cost for a particular uncertainty model and an extension to kernels.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a clustering framework for graphs whose connections encode pairwise similarities among data points. Membership is soft and probabilistic, so the representation can express uncertainty or overlap in how points belong to groups. This provides a flexible way to describe clustering structure using the similarities already represented by the graph.

A hierarchy emerges naturally within the framework: lower-level clusters gradually merge into higher-level ones. The authors analyze this hierarchy using random walks on the graph. Higher levels statistically model diffusion over longer periods, so they capture more global patterns of connectivity. The hierarchy therefore has an interpretation tied to how information spreads through the similarity structure.

This interpretation connects clustering resolution with diffusion time. Shorter-range structure appears at lower levels, while broader groupings emerge through longer-term diffusion. The authors report very encouraging experimental results. The stated contribution is a unified framework for probabilistic membership and hierarchical grouping, with the random-walk analysis explaining why different levels expose different scales of organization.
neurips-2005-soft-clustering-on-graphs-3.tldr: A probabilistic graph-clustering framework naturally builds a hierarchy whose higher levels reflect longer-term diffusion and more global structure.

paragraphs: Temporal-difference networks represent an agent's knowledge through linked predictions about interactions with its environment. Those predictions can be defined using other predictions and can ask what would happen if the agent took a particular action. This paper extends the framework from predictions tied to successive time steps toward predictions spanning longer intervals.

The extension places temporally abstract options on the links of the question network. Options describe extended ways of behaving, allowing a prediction to depend on an entire course of behavior rather than only a single action. This broadens the kinds of conditional questions the network can represent while retaining its compositional structure.

The primary algorithmic contribution is an intra-option learning method for these networks that incorporates function approximation and eligibility traces. The authors present empirical examples demonstrating the algorithm's effectiveness and the greater expressive power of the temporally abstract networks. The result is both a richer language for an agent's predictions and a learning procedure for predictions conditioned on behavior unfolding over time.
neurips-2005-temporal-abstraction-in-tem.tldr: Temporally abstract options let TD networks predict outcomes of extended behaviors, supported by a new intra-option learning algorithm and empirical examples.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how to automatically build representations for approximating value functions in Markov decision processes. Its starting point is the structure and topology of the state space. When states can be represented as a graph or manifold, that organization can guide the construction of basis functions used to express a value function.

The authors explore two approaches. One uses eigenfunctions of the Laplacian, providing a graph analogue of global Fourier analysis. The other uses diffusion wavelets, extending wavelet ideas to graphs through multiple scales defined by powers of a diffusion operator or random walk. Both derive representation elements from relationships among states.

The approaches offer different ways to organize approximation around state-space structure: one uses global spectral functions, while the other introduces scales through diffusion. The authors present them as a foundation for methods addressing large Markov decision processes in which representations and policies are learned together. The contribution is therefore about constructing the ingredients of value-function approximation automatically, rather than taking the representation as fixed in advance.
neurips-2005-value-function-approximatio.tldr: Laplacian eigenfunctions and diffusion wavelets construct value-function bases from state-space geometry, supporting joint learning of representations and policies.

paragraphs: This paper studies models containing hidden variables whose distributions are non-Gaussian. Its focus is on criteria for representing those variables variationally and on deriving expectation-maximization algorithms in a general form. The aim is to describe a broad approach to this class of models rather than derive a procedure only for one particular example.

The central theoretical result establishes a general equivalence among convex bounding methods, evidence-based methods, and ensemble learning or Variational Bayes methods. These are different formulations for handling the latent-variable problem. Showing an equivalence connects their mathematical roles and provides a common account of methods that might otherwise be considered separately.

According to the abstract, such equivalences had previously been demonstrated only in particular cases. Extending the connection to a general formulation is therefore the main advance, alongside the variational EM derivations. Its significance is a unified understanding of these approaches to non-Gaussian latent-variable models, rather than an empirical claim that one named method outperforms the others.
neurips-2005-variational-em-algorithms-f.tldr: The paper derives general variational EM algorithms and establishes an equivalence among convex bounding, evidence-based, and Variational Bayes approaches.
